correctness.rationale: For odd m, multiplicativity and the explicit alternating geometric sum show beta(m) is a power of two iff m is squarefree product of prime Fermat numbers; even odd-prime exponents give an odd factor, odd exponents above 1 also carry an odd factor. If 2 beta(beta(p^a))=p^a, parity forces p=2. For even a, odd d=a+1 excludes all Fermat divisors except F0=3 and forces a=2. For odd a, d=a+1=2^t v, each Fermat prime factor of (2^d-1)/3 has index <t; size comparison with product_{j<t}F_j=2^(2^t)-1 forces v=1. Squarefree Fermat-prime factorization then requires t<=5 because F5 is composite. Exponents 1,2,3,7,15,31 satisfy the equality; independent direct beta computations confirm 1..24 and exponent 31. The argument, not the finite check, proves all prime powers.

originality.rationale: Tóth 2011 Section 7 proves the condition within the specially selected 2^(2^t-1) family and lists six examples, but does not establish the converse that every prime power satisfying 2 beta(beta(n))=n belongs to that family, with additional a=2. OEIS A200758 is an example list, not a completeness theorem. Published related alternating-divisor prime-support constraints are about different equations or do not imply this converse. Earlier equivalent unpublished Fermat-divisor argument remains possible.
residual_risks: No claim about products of distinct primes; this is only the prime-power family.

The Fermat-prime factor restriction explains exactly why familiar examples stop and adds the exceptional fourth power. It is not a mere recomputation of a finite OEIS list.
